title: Show HN: Stop applying to jobs using AI-generated resume
author: grandimam
snippet: When LLMs hands you a resume or pdf it carry markers of how it was made, including the source. You can't see them on the page but applicant tracking systems can read it. So recruiters are flagging such profiles and rejecting them entirely. I had tested this across 40+ AI models…
excerpt: When LLMs hands you a resume or pdf it carry markers of how it was made, including the source. You can't see them on the page but applicant tracking systems can read it. So recruiters are flagging such profiles and rejecting them entirely. I had tested this across 40+ AI models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, etc) to produce a resume and every single file carried a marker. To solve this problem. I had built a free tool to show what your file says and gives you a cleaned version: - Drop your resume and get a cleaned copy - Free, no account. What it doesn't do: it won't rewrite your resume or make AI-sounding wording more human. It only deals with what's hidden in the file. It's a simple tool, but it feels absolutely necessary now as more people are using AI for generating their entire resume or even editing them. I am the developer, happy to answer any questions.

snippet: Release v5.24.0 New Model additions Inkling 2 Mini Inkling 2 Mini is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is a smaller sibling of Inkling 2 Small, added in v5.23.0. It has 24 decoder layers instead of…
excerpt: Release v5.24.0 New Model additions Inkling 2 Mini Inkling 2 Mini is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is a smaller sibling of Inkling 2 Small, added in v5.23.0. It has 24 decoder layers instead of 48, and compensates with a looping mechanism in which layers 6 to 17 run three times. A learned message-passing mechanism mixes the residuals of the previous pass into the attention and mixture-of-experts inputs of each loop layer. The decoder has a hidden size of 2304 and routes each token to 8 of 128 experts. The image encoder, tokenizer and processor are the same as Inkling 2 Small's. A research checkpoint (TML-d24-varloop-research) has the same architecture but supports a variable number of loop passes. Fewer passes are faster, and more passes improve quality. Both checkpoints contain NVFP4 and MXFP8 quantized layers, which are dequantized at load time. Links: Documentation | Blog Post | HF Blog Post Add Inkling2 Mini (#51050) by @guarin Apertus 1.5 Apertus 1.5 is a multimodal model from the Swiss AI Initiative that accepts text, images and audio and generates text. It extends the Apertus language model with the EMU3.5 vision tokenizer for images and WavTokenizer for audio. The EMU3.5 tokenizer is an image-only VQGAN with the same encoder as Chameleon's, and it assigns codes by the largest inner product with the codebook. The media tokenizers turn images and audio into discrete tokens, which the language backbone processes alongside text in a shared input vocabulary. The output vocabulary contains only text tokens, so image and audio generation are not supported. title: Show HN: Accounting built like Git, with files in your own storage
author: oskar77
snippet: Lots of ways to do your accounting today with LLMs, but for some reason there is this expectation you are suppose to keep the old accounting software around? And it sort of makes sense, they vouch for the ledger integrity and keep the audit trail. It reminded me of how things…
excerpt: Lots of ways to do your accounting today with LLMs, but for some reason there is this expectation you are suppose to keep the old accounting software around? And it sort of makes sense, they vouch for the ledger integrity and keep the audit trail. It reminded me of how things where like before git. You trusted the host not just to keep the data but to vouch for the versioning, and what git really did was move that last part into the data itself. Accounting ledgers need integrity, in fact it is mandated by law in most places. Git buys integrity by publishing, because if you do not share your repo with anyone, you can always force push and rewrite the commit history and no-one would know. But your books are sensitive and cannot be published. So I made git-style versioning for double-entry accounting. Entries gets hashed and timestamped, service checks for debit equals credit, and it ends up as json files you keep in your own S3 bucket. Not in a vendor database. For the hosted version the access keys to the buckets are encrypted with the user passkey / assistant OAuth, so the service cannot read anything at-rest. For user convenience there is a hosted version where you do the books through MCP on whatever LLM you already use. The whole thing is so cheap to run, because the service does not store any sensitive data, so it is free, although you need an AI client with MCP support and an S3 bucket.
